notes: CPR 3.9 relief against strike-out; circuit judge's contradictory order redetermined on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Welsh v Parnianzadeh: relief from strike-out after solicitor defaults
key_facts: The claimant alleged she fell on a wet defective floor at the defendant's Southern Fried Chicken shop in February 2000 but did not issue proceedings until near the limitation expiry.

After repeated defaults by several firms of solicitors and litigant-in-person delays, District Judge Morris struck out the claim on 19 January 2004 for failure to comply with an unless order requiring particulars, a medical report and schedule of loss.
On appeal, HHJ Dangor dismissed the appeal but gave case management directions to continue the claim with interest penalties, producing a contradictory order.
The Court of Appeal redetermined the appeal, finding the district judge had failed to apply CPR 3.9/3.4 discretion properly and that a fair trial remained possible.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a circuit judge's order dismissing an appeal from a district judge's strike-out of a personal injury claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the strike-out was set aside and the claim permitted to continue on terms similar to those proposed by the circuit judge, with no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where relief against an unless order or strike-out is sought, the court must exercise discretion under CPR 3.9 or 3.4 by reference to the checklist including fault, explanation, prejudice and proportionality; persistent solicitor default and a litigant's own persistence may justify relief even after long delay if no real prejudice to the defendant is shown and a fair trial remains possible.
legal_issues: Whether the circuit judge could dismiss an appeal from strike-out yet give directions continuing the claim
Whether District Judge Morris should have applied CPR 3.9 rather than treating the matter as a bare unless-order default
Whether relief from sanction was disproportionate given limitation and repeated non-compliance
Whether Article 6 added anything beyond the CPR discretion
linked_authorities: Hansom v Rex Makin & Co [2003] EWCA Civ 1801
Flaxmann-Binns v Lincolnshire County Council [2004] EWCA Civ 424

confidence.notes: Full appellate reasoning on discretion and final remedial order are clearly recorded.

notes: SPC Article 3(d) appeal; Patents Court referred interpretation questions to CJEU alongside MIT reference.

enrichment.short_title: Yissum v Comptroller: SPC for calcitriol topical psoriasis product
key_facts: Yissum sought a supplementary protection certificate for calcitriol based on European Patent (UK) No 0129003B2 covering topical dermatological use of cholecalciferol derivatives.

The UK marketing authorisation for Silkis ointment (3 µg calcitriol per gram) was granted in December 2001, but earlier UK authorisations existed for Calcijex and Rocaltrol containing calcitriol for other routes and indications.
The hearing officer refused the SPC on Article 3(d) grounds, rejecting both calcitriol alone and calcitriol-plus-ointment-base formulations as the 'product'.
On appeal Yissum advanced a new primary case defining the product as calcitriol for topical treatment of psoriasis.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Patents Court from a Comptroller hearing officer decision refusing an SPC application.
enrichment.outcome: The court exercised its discretion to refer questions on Article 1(b) interpretation to the Court of Justice, noting the pending MIT reference and that the issues were not acte claire.
enrichment.ratio: Where the meaning of 'product' and 'combination of active ingredients' in Article 1(b) of Regulation 1768/92 is uncertain—especially for second medical use patents and formulation-dependent efficacy—the Patents Court may refer to the CJEU rather than decide, particularly when a related reference is already pending.
legal_issues: Whether 'product' in Article 1(b) includes therapeutic use or only the pharmacologically active ingredient
Whether calcitriol with an ointment base is a combination of active ingredients
Whether Article 3(d) bars an SPC where calcitriol was previously authorised in other medicinal products
Whether Pharmacia Italia made the interpretation acte claire
linked_authorities: Farmitalia Carlo Erba srl's SPC Application (C-392/97)

confidence.notes: Procedural outcome is a CJEU reference; substantive SPC entitlement remains undecided.

notes: Trial judgment for restitution after Canadian property investment fraud; defendant found serially dishonest.

enrichment.short_title: Patel v Naik: recovery of misappropriated Canadian property investment funds
key_facts: Mr Patel, a taxi driver, paid £54,266.55 to Mr Naik between 1999 and 2000 to invest in Canadian property and syndicated portfolios after being introduced through a mutual friend.
Payments included £30,000 to Belgravia Property Developments Ltd, cheques to Naik and Plasto Ltd, cash and a C$20,000 transfer to Turling Property Services (Canada) Inc.
Naik repeatedly denied receipt and knowledge of the companies and accounts despite documentary evidence linking him to Belgravia, Plasto and Turling.
Patel's consistent evidence and documentation were preferred; the court found the monies were never invested and had been misappropriated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of a claim for restitution for total failure of consideration alternatively damages for repudiatory breach after prolonged litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for the claimant for £54,266.55 plus interest; the defendant was liable to account and repay on a restitutionary basis.
enrichment.ratio: Where an investor pays money to a self-professed property adviser for investment at his direction and the adviser misappropriates the funds, the investor may recover the sums on the basis that consideration has wholly failed, notwithstanding shifting and dishonest defences.
legal_issues: Whether agreements existed for investment in Canadian property through the defendant personally
Whether payments to Belgravia, Plasto and Turling were at the defendant's direction
Whether the defendant was liable despite attributing dealings to Turling as his employer
Whether the source of cash payments affected the claim

confidence.notes: Detailed findings of fact and clear judgment for the full sum claimed.

notes: Pension consent breach appeal; employer role under 1994 rules and 50% loss-of-chance damages upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Kelly v Mersey Docks: employer consent to ill-health pension
key_facts: Miss Kelly, a survey plotter employed since 1971, developed wrist and upper limb problems from 1993 and was dismissed on medical grounds in August 1995.
Under amended 1994 pension fund rules she needed employer consent to retire by reason of partial incapacity before trustees could award an ill-health pension.
The Harbour Company refused consent and applied a merits test rather than asking whether trustees might reasonably award a pension; she lost the chance of a partial incapacity pension.
The judge assessed her lost chance at 50%; the Court of Appeal held the employer's role was a filter not primary decision-maker and upheld the percentage.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against judgment for damages to be assessed for breach of an implied term not arbitrarily to refuse consent to ill-health retirement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; damages for loss of a 50% chance of obtaining a partial incapacity pension were upheld and limitation defences rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Under the 1994 Mersey Docks pension rules the employer's consent function was to decide whether there was a real prospect the trustees would find partial or total incapacity, not to adjudicate the merits itself; arbitrary refusal breached contract and entitled the employee to damages for loss of the chance of a trustee award.
legal_issues: Whether dismissal could amount to retirement with employer consent under Rule 9.b
Whether the employer or trustees had primary responsibility for incapacity decisions
What test governed the employer's consent under the 1994 rules
Whether rules 17 and 18 excluded liability and whether the claim was time-barred
linked_authorities: Allied Maples Group Ltd v Simmons & Simmons [1995] 1 WLR 1602

confidence.notes: Complex pension construction and damages assessment are fully reasoned though medically contested.

notes: Post-dismissal costs judgment correcting double-counting in permission-to-appeal cost assessment.

enrichment.short_title: Challinor v Challinor: costs of refused ancillary relief permission appeal
key_facts: Following dismissal of the appellant's application for permission to appeal Wilson J's ancillary relief orders, the respondent sought summary assessment of her costs.
The appellant, acting in person, had raised disclosure allegations against the respondent that should have been pursued at trial.
The court directed written submissions on costs and rejected the appellant's argument for no order as to costs.
On reconsideration the court corrected a £960 double-counting error in document preparation costs, reducing the assessment to £16,714 inclusive of VAT.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Written determination of costs after refusal of permission to appeal in divorce ancillary relief proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: The appellant was ordered to pay £16,714 inclusive of VAT, to be deducted from the lump sum payable to him under Wilson J's order.
enrichment.ratio: Where permission to appeal in ancillary relief proceedings is refused after allegations of non-disclosure are raised for the first time on appeal, costs follow the event and the respondent is entitled to costs reasonably incurred in answering those allegations, subject to fair adjustment of any billing discrepancies.
legal_issues: Whether any costs order should be made against a litigant in person
Which of competing schedules of costs should form the basis of assessment
Whether document preparation costs were double-counted across schedules
Whether transcribers' fees should be deducted where the appellant supplied a transcript

confidence.notes: Final costs figure and mechanism of payment are explicitly stated.

notes: Asylum appeal remitted after IAT overturned airport-only reasoning without addressing home-region persecution finding.

enrichment.short_title: Tezgel v SSHD: Alevi Kurd asylum and internal relocation remittal
key_facts: Mr Tezgel, an Alevi Kurd, claimed asylum after arriving in the UK in June 2001, citing repeated detentions, beatings and ill-treatment in Turkey.
After a brain haemorrhage in January 2002 he remained in fragile health; the adjudicator allowed the appeal on airport questioning risk and on broader Convention grounds.
The IAT held the airport scenario was evidentially unsupported and allowed the Secretary of State's appeal on that ground alone.

The Court of Appeal found paragraph 24 of the adjudicator's determination also amounted to a finding of well-founded fear of persecution at home on race and religion grounds, which the IAT had not addressed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision allowing the Secretary of State's appeal from an adjudicator.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted, appeal allowed and the case remitted to the IAT to consider risk of persecution, Article 3 treatment and internal relocation.
enrichment.ratio: Where an adjudicator's determination contains a distinct finding of well-founded fear of persecution for Refugee Convention reasons in the home region, an tribunal cannot uphold an appeal based only on rejecting a separate airport-entry scenario without considering whether that home-region finding was vitiated by error of law.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator's airport-return findings were evidentially supported
Whether paragraph 24 extended beyond airport risks to home-region persecution
Whether the IAT erred by failing to address internal relocation and post-airport risk
Whether the appellant abandoned reliance on home-region persecution before the IAT
linked_authorities: Subesh v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 56

confidence.notes: Appellate disposition to remit is clear though underlying persecution merits remain for the IAT.

notes: Section 67 appeal; arbitration clause construed to cover outgoing partner goodwill dispute.

enrichment.short_title: Ellis v Coleman: arbitration jurisdiction after partner retirement
key_facts: Mr Coleman retired from a motorcycle and van courier partnership trading as JCA International under an agreement dated 1 April 2002 executed in March 2003.
Continuing partners Ellis and Hume exercised an option to purchase his share; dispute arose whether goodwill payment was due.
Coleman referred the dispute to arbitration; the arbitrator held he had jurisdiction but the continuing partners appealed under section 67.
The agreement's arbitration clause and definition of 'Partners' were argued to exclude disputes with an outgoing partner after the succession date.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 67 appeal against an arbitrator's ruling that the partnership arbitration clause covered a goodwill dispute with a retired partner.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the arbitrator had jurisdiction because clause 33 was intended to cover all partnership disputes and 'Partners' should not be read literally to exclude outgoing partners.
enrichment.ratio: An arbitration clause requiring referral of disputes touching the partnership or the construction of the agreement should be construed commercially to include disputes between continuing and outgoing partners over post-retirement buy-out terms, notwithstanding a literal definition of 'Partners' as current members only.
legal_issues: Whether a dispute after retirement was between 'Partners' as defined
Whether the arbitration clause covered construction of the buy-out option
Whether a temporal cut-off excluded outgoing partner claims
Whether Investors Compensation Scheme principles permitted departure from literal wording
linked_authorities: Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896
Sirius International Insurance Co v FAI General Insurance Ltd [2004] UKHL 54

confidence.notes: Jurisdictional question and construction approach are clearly decided.

notes: Reinsurance arbitration appeal; Cigna award coverage finding not an issue estoppel against Lincoln.

enrichment.short_title: Sun Life v Lincoln: issue estoppel and confidential arbitration awards
key_facts: Sun/Phoenix lost a Cigna arbitration in which Occ/Acc reinsurances were avoided for broker misrepresentation but the tribunal also stated the Unicover book would have been covered absent avoidance.
In a separate Lincoln arbitration Sun/Phoenix contended Unicover losses were recoverable from Lincoln under an earlier NRL reinsurance only if the Cigna reinsurances would have covered them.
Lincoln argued the Cigna tribunal's coverage finding bound Sun/Phoenix; Toulson J held the Lincoln tribunal could not depart from it.
The Lincoln tribunal had reached the opposite factual conclusion on coverage but was overturned on the estoppel point.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a High Court decision that a prior Cigna arbitration award created a binding issue estoppel in a later Lincoln reinsurance arbitration.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; paragraph 4 of the Lincoln award was restored in the form decided by the Lincoln tribunal; the Cigna coverage finding did not estop Sun/Phoenix against Lincoln.
enrichment.ratio: A determination in a private arbitration between X and Y that Y would have covered certain risks but for avoidance is collateral to the award and does not create an issue estoppel usable by a non-party Z in a later arbitration; only necessary fundamental determinations bind parties, and strangers cannot treat private arbitral opinions as conclusive.
legal_issues: Whether the Cigna tribunal decided Unicover was covered apart from avoidance
Whether that decision was necessary or collateral/obiter
Whether issue estoppel or Saville J's Moundreas principle bound Sun/Phoenix in the Lincoln arbitration
Whether the Lincoln tribunal's analysis of the Cigna award was reviewable as law
linked_authorities: Good Challenger Navegante SA v Metalexportimport SA (The Good Challenger) [2004] 1 Lloyd's Rep 67
Fidelitas Shipping Co Ltd v V/O Exportchleb [1966] 1 QB 630
Moundreas v Steamship Mutual Underwriting Association (Bermuda) Ltd [1995] 2 Lloyd's Rep 515

confidence.notes: Appellate ratio on estoppel and final order are explicit though reinsurance facts are complex.

notes: Winding-up petition injunction; bona fide set-off dispute over missing train batteries.

enrichment.short_title: Alstom v Elequip: restraining winding-up petition over disputed debt
key_facts: Elequip, in administrative receivership, supplied West Coast Main Line tilting train equipment to Alstom under a 2000 agreement.
On 17 October 2003 the parties agreed Alstom would pay £730,000 for release of scheduled goods, including £500,000 immediately and £230,000 by 24 October.
Alstom discovered many batteries missing from delivered rafts and J Car material and withheld the £230,000 balance, asserting cross-claims exceeding the petition debt.
Elequip threatened a winding-up petition for £86,631.20; Alstom sought an injunction restraining presentation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to restrain presentation of a winding-up petition based on an alleged debt disputed on substantial cross-claim grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction granted; Alstom showed a bona fide substantial dispute including whether October 2003 letters incorporated no-set-off terms and whether Schedule 1 cross-claims could be set off against Schedule 2 sums.
enrichment.ratio: Where a petition debt arises from a post-receivership bespoke agreement negotiated before a general no-set-off receivership letter was signed, there is a seriously arguable case that the debt is not payable without set-off for missing goods and related misrepresentation, so presentation of a winding-up petition should be restrained.
legal_issues: Whether the 17 October agreement was standalone or incorporated the 16 October no-set-off letter
Whether Alstom had a cross-claim for missing batteries on Schedule 1 items
Whether set-off was available across pre- and post-receivership contracts
Whether the dispute was bona fide and substantial for Re Bayoil purposes
linked_authorities: Montgomery v Wanda Modes Ltd [2002] 1 BCLC 289

confidence.notes: Interlocutory findings on disputed debt and cross-claim are clearly reasoned.

notes: Lands Tribunal jurisdiction appeal; lease user covenants held restrictive not positive.

enrichment.short_title: Blumenthal v Church Commissioners: Lands Tribunal jurisdiction over user covenants
key_facts: The tenant held a long lease of 1 Hyde Park Gardens with user covenants restricting use to specified residential and former Royal Society of Literature layouts.
A 2001 deed of variation permitted parts formerly used by the Royal Society of Literature to be used as private residential flats.
The tenant applied under section 84 to modify covenants further to incorporate basement areas into single dwellings.
The landlord contended the covenants were positive obligations to keep and use premises in specified ways, outside the Lands Tribunal's jurisdiction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Lands Tribunal preliminary ruling that section 84 jurisdiction existed over disputed lease user covenants.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the covenants were restrictive in substance and the Lands Tribunal had jurisdiction to consider modification.
enrichment.ratio: Lease covenants requiring premises to be kept and used for particular residential purposes are properly construed as restrictive covenants affecting user within section 84, not positive obligations requiring continuous occupation, especially where literal positive construction would expose a tenant to forfeiture for events beyond their control such as a sub-tenant vacating.
legal_issues: Whether clause 13 user covenants were positive or restrictive
Whether leaving premises idle between tenancies would breach positive covenants
Whether section 84 applies only to restrictions arising under covenant as to use
How to distinguish positive obligations excluded from Lands Tribunal jurisdiction
linked_authorities: Westminster City Council v Duke of Westminster [1991] 4 All ER 136
Abbey Homesteads (Developments) Ltd v Northamptonshire County Council [1986] 1 EGLR 24

confidence.notes: Preliminary jurisdiction point and covenant construction are fully reasoned on appeal.
